explain.what: Whether the share price is above or below its average price over the last ~10 months.
explain.why: Big funds buy and sell around this line, so being above it usually means buyers are in control. It is slow: it confirms a turn after it has happened.
explain.score: The price is above its long-run average: the long-term trend is up.

explain.what: Whether the shorter trend (last ~10 weeks) is running above or below the longer trend (last ~10 months).
explain.why: It shows whether the trend itself is turning, not just where the price is today.
explain.score: The shorter trend is above the longer one: momentum is building upward.

indicators.name: Relative strength vs peers, 3 months
indicators.measured: equal-weighted average of 6 peers over 63 trading days

explain.what: Whether the stock has done better or worse than its direct competitors over the last 3 months.
explain.why: It separates something specific to this company from a whole-industry move.
explain.score: Beating its competitors: the market is rewarding this company in particular.

indicators.name: Buying vs selling volume
indicators.measured: volume on up days ÷ down days, last 20 trading days

explain.what: Whether more shares change hands on days the price rises than on days it falls (last 20 trading days).
explain.why: Large investors leave footprints in trading volume; heavy buying days suggest they are accumulating.
explain.score: Much more trading on up days: buyers are more active than sellers.

explain.what: How many shares are borrowed and sold by investors betting the price will fall, and whether that is growing.
explain.why: Short sellers often do deep research, so a rising number of bets against a stock is a warning worth noticing.
explain.score: Bets against the stock are steady.

indicators.name: Institutional ownership change
indicators.measured: shares added minus shares cut by institutions last quarter, as % of shares outstanding
indicators.note: Proxy: counts changes in existing positions, not new or closed ones.

explain.what: Whether professional investment firms, in total, added or cut shares last quarter.
explain.why: Shows whether the big money is moving in or out. It arrives late (filings come up to 45 days after the quarter).
explain.score: Funds added a meaningful number of shares last quarter.

indicators.name: Dollar backdrop (shared macro)
indicators.measured: the dollar index 20 trading days earlier

explain.what: Whether the US dollar has strengthened or weakened over the last month.
explain.why: A strong dollar pulls money out of riskier assets worldwide and shrinks the dollar value of overseas sales.
explain.score: The dollar has strengthened: a headwind for stocks.

indicators.name: Fed rate expectations (shared macro)
indicators.measured: net odds (cut minus rise) for the next Fed meeting, 28 days earlier
indicators.note: Now: 1% cut, 18% rise; a month ago: 5% cut, 28% rise.

explain.what: Whether markets now expect the Fed to cut or raise interest rates at its next meeting, compared with a month ago.
explain.why: Interest rates set the price of every other asset; expectations move long before the Fed acts.

indicators.name: Revenue growth trend
indicators.measured: average growth of the prior 4 quarters, each vs a year earlier

explain.what: Whether sales growth is speeding up or slowing down compared with the past year.
explain.why: The plainest evidence of whether customers want more of what the company sells.

explain.what: How much investors pay for each dollar of the company's expected profit, compared with its competitors.
explain.why: Paying much more than for rivals means good news is already in the price, so there is less room for disappointment.
explain.score: Much more expensive than its competitors: the price assumes things keep going very well.

explain.what: The same comparison as above, but allowing for how fast profits are expected to grow.
explain.why: A higher price can be fair if profits grow faster; this checks whether they do.

explain.what: The company's total value (including debt) compared with its operating profit, against competitors.
explain.why: Unlike the P/E, this counts debt, so an indebted company cannot look artificially cheap.

lead: AMD reads Buy at +50 on a −100 to +100 scale, unchanged from +50 on 1 Oct (Buy line +30): demand and the price trend score the maximum, but investors already pay a steep premium, and the reading depends on AI spending and the price momentum both holding up.
bullets: Demand is at full strength, but it is one bet. Demand scores +100: revenue grew 50.1% vs a year earlier, faster than its 34.8% average of the prior four quarters; Data Center grew 107% and PC chips 22.5% (Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier), and the big-4 cloud firms' capital spending 77%. Guidance (40.6% growth) beat the roughly 35.6% expected, and the 2027 earnings forecast rose 18.3% in 90 days ($15.58 vs $13.18 a share). Almost all of these track AI data-centre spending, so a pause there would turn them together. Gross margin is up 5.6 points (last 4 quarters vs the 4 a year earlier), but about 2.7 points of that comes from a one-off $800m China chip write-down in the year-ago figures.

It is priced for it, before counting dilution. Valuation scores −63: investors pay 45% more per dollar of expected next-12-month profit than the peer median (46.6x vs 32.2x forward P/E). On company value including debt vs last-12-month operating profit before depreciation (EV/EBITDA) it is 107.3x vs 30.5x, a gap overstated because AMD's revenue is growing 50% a year. Only the growth-adjusted P/E is in line (0.6 vs 0.7, 11% below the peer median). Not scored: warrants to OpenAI and Meta could add up to 320m shares (about 20% of today's), which would lift the forward P/E to about 54x if all vested.

The money backdrop is mixed. Liquidity scores +40: volume on up days is 3.73x that on down days (last 20 trading days) and institutions already holding AMD added a net 3.80% of shares last quarter (new and closed positions not counted), but the dollar index is 2.92 points higher than 20 trading days ago and markets now give an 18% chance of a Fed rate rise on 28 Oct, down from 28% a month earlier.

The trend is strongly up, and stretched. Price scores +100: AMD is 69.2% above its 200-day average and 11.6 points ahead of its peers over the last 3 months; it closed at $633.91, +2.95% on the day vs +0.73% for the S&P 500. That distance trips the stretch flag: a sign the run may be overextended and prone to sharp pullbacks (timing context only, not scored). The Buy leans on momentum: with a neutral price trend the composite would be about +25, which is Hold.
Not yet a confirmed call. Day 4 of the 10 trading days of score history needed. Next big test: results, expected 3 Nov (date not yet announced).
defects: Staging build, fourth day of history: the call needs 10 trading days of scores before it can be confirmed.
VL3 (P/E vs own history) is removed for AMD and left out of the score (applied by the shared engine from 30 Sep): trailing P/E is distorted by 2023 losses and Xilinx amortisation.

EV/EBITDA uses last-12-month EBITDA (free source); for a company growing 50% a year this makes AMD look expensive. Debt in EV ($4.3bn) includes leases (Yahoo); AMD reports $3.2bn of borrowings, a 0.1% effect on EV.
Forward P/E uses 2027 earnings forecasts (AMD's next fiscal year), not strictly the next 12 months; peers use their own next fiscal years, which end at different dates.

Gross margin trend (DM6) uses reported margins: the year-ago 4 quarters include a one-off $800m MI308 write-down, which adds about 2.7 of the 5.6-point rise. DM6 would still score bullish without it (about +2.9 points).
OpenAI and Meta warrants (up to 320m shares, about 20% of today's shares) are not reflected in P/E or any score; see shareholder notes.

segments.name: Data Center
segments.sells: EPYC server processors, Instinct AI chips (MI350, MI450, Helios racks), Pensando networking chips and data-center FPGAs.
segments.buyers: Cloud giants and AI labs (Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, OpenAI, Anthropic), governments and large companies.
pos: Highest growth: +107% in the Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier (+55% over the last 4 quarters); now most of AMD's revenue.
Margin rising: 29% segment operating margin over the last 4 quarters vs 21% a year earlier (31% in the latest quarter).
Multi-year supply deals (OpenAI up to 6 GW, Meta up to 6 GW, Anthropic up to 2 GW) give more visibility than one-off orders.
Server processors are sticky: customers standardise on a platform for years.
neg: Not recurring: hardware sold per order, no subscription income.
Concentrated: a handful of very large buyers decide most orders, and they negotiate hard on price.

Some demand is supported by AMD's own shares and money: OpenAI and Meta get up to 160m AMD shares each as they take delivery, and AMD is investing up to $5bn in Anthropic alongside its 2 GW commitment.
Tied to the AI spending cycle (chain C1); a pause in AI budgets hits here first.
Export rules can wipe out profit quickly: an $800m China charge turned the segment to a loss in Q2 2025.
Full racks (Helios) include more bought-in parts such as memory, which may lower the margin percentage (a risk, not yet seen).

segments.name: Client
segments.sells: Ryzen processors for desktop and laptop PCs, including AI PC chips.
segments.buyers: PC makers (Lenovo, HP, Dell, Asus) and PC builders; ultimately consumers and businesses.
pos: Taking share from Intel: +23% in the Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier while the PC market is squeezed.
Big and familiar brand; helps AMD sell to the same business customers in servers.
neg: Lower margin: 18% segment operating margin (Client and Gaming combined, last 4 quarters), about 11 points below Data Center.
One-off, seasonal consumer sales; nothing recurring.
Price competition from Intel, Qualcomm and now NVIDIA (RTX Spark PC chips from autumn 2026).
Memory price rises make PCs dearer, which can cut demand (chain C2).

segments.name: Gaming
segments.sells: Custom chips for Sony PlayStation and Microsoft Xbox consoles, and Radeon graphics cards.
pos: Console chips come from multi-year contracts with Sony and Microsoft: predictable volumes and little extra R&D.
A new console generation would lift revenue again (timing not announced).
neg: Shrinking now: −31% in the Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier, as current consoles are late in their life (though +30% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before, after the 2025 console ramp).
Thin margins: the gaming part earned 3-18% operating margin in 2022-24, when AMD still reported it separately.
Graphics cards lose share to NVIDIA.

segments.name: Embedded
segments.sells: Xilinx FPGAs and adaptive chips, plus embedded Ryzen and EPYC, for factories, cars, telecoms, medical, aerospace and defence.
segments.buyers: Thousands of equipment makers (industrial, auto, communications, defence).
pos: Highest segment margin: 37% over the last 4 quarters.
The closest thing AMD has to recurring revenue: chips are designed into equipment that is built and sold for 10+ years.
Many small customers: no single buyer dominates.
Steady cash generator with low extra investment.
neg: Slow growth: +5% over the last 4 quarters vs +40% for AMD as a whole; the latest quarter (+19% vs a year earlier) is a rebound from a low base.
Margin falling: 37% vs 50% three years earlier (last 4 quarters each).
Swings with customers' stock levels: revenue fell 46% from Q1 2023 to Q1 2024 as customers ran down inventories.
Now only 9% of revenue (last 4 quarters), so it cushions the company less than it did in 2023.

pos: Fastest-growing part (Data Center, +55% vs a year earlier) earns above the company segment operating margin.
neg: The shift in mix alone took 0.4 pts off segment operating margin vs a year earlier (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters a year earlier, each part's margin held at that earlier level).
The shift in mix alone took 3.5 pts off segment operating margin vs 3 years earlier (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters 3 years earlier, each part's margin held at that earlier level).
Partly recurring revenue (long-life contracts or design wins) down 17 pts in 3 years to 9% of sales (last 4 quarters).
Concentration: Data Center is 54% of sales (last 4 quarters).

shift.title: What the shift means for AMD
pos: Higher profit per dollar of sales, but not from the mix: segment operating margin rose to 26% (last 4 quarters) from 21% a year earlier because Data Center's own margin rose (29% vs 21%). The shift in mix itself took about 0.4 points off, because high-margin Embedded shrank.
Free cash flow was 18.7% of revenue over the last 4 quarters ($7.7bn) vs 11.8% a year earlier ($3.5bn).
Faster growth: revenue is up 115% in three years (Jun 2026 quarter vs Jun 2023 quarter), almost all from Data Center.
neg: Less diversified: Data Center is 54% of revenue over the last 4 quarters (58% in the Jun 2026 quarter), up from 27% three years earlier. A slowdown in AI budgets would hit AMD harder than before.
Less recurring: the steadiest business (Embedded) fell from 26% to 9% of revenue, and Gaming from 30% to 9% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters to Jun 2023).
More concentrated: a few very large customers now drive most growth, which gives them pricing power; two of them hold warrants for AMD shares.

mix.note: Segment operating margin = the segment's operating profit ÷ its revenue, before company-wide costs AMD does not allocate (mainly amortisation of Xilinx purchase intangibles and share-based pay). AMD reports Client and Gaming profit only combined from 2025 (2024 restated the same way), so both show the combined margin.
